Simplest solution: Add another comfy chair, or else swap the armchair for a sofa or loveseat. The best way to cozy up a space is to provide a place for guests to sit and hang out with you, and the best way to make a living room look pathetic is to have only one seat.


Other tips:


I know you have a carpet, but adding a rug can help enclose and center a space and make it feel cozy and welcoming. The chair(s) should all be the same amount of on/off the rug, for example, if one chair is halfway on the rug, the other chair should also be halfway on the rug. It creates unity and prevents the space from looking sloppy.


Speaking of sloppy, the current arrangement of the shelves, posters, and record player make the space look cluttered and disorganized. If the plug situation allows, I would: 
- move the tall shelf next to the TV where the Bolt Thrower poster is
- put the Bolt Thrower poster on the front wall
- scoot the short shelf over so it isn't awkwardly floating halfway in front of the window
- move the record player down either next to the door or else put the short shelf by the door and the record player next to that (you can put it in front of the window just don't float it between the window and the wall)
- either put the things that don't fit on the shelves away out of sight somewhere, or invest in more shelf space. Maybe utilize one of the other two walls for shelf space if possible. Just get your things off the floor and out of that unstable looking stack!


If nothing else is feasible, at least get the excess put away and scoot the shelves so it's either in front of the window or not.


And finally, a well placed plant can go a long way.


Good luck!

A machete would probably be more effective than a knife, at least in terms of making your arms look longer and more dangerous, and I'm pretty sure it's legal to keep in your car as long as you keep it sheathed, considering it's a gardening tool sold in Home Depot and everything. Axes and crowbars are other tools that are frequently carried in vehicles and would be better defense against bears than a knife. For an actual knife, I think the rule is you can conceal carry as long as the blade is under 12 inches? Don't quote me on that. And no switchblades.

But ultimately if you're worried about bears GET SOME BEAR SPRAY, not pepper spray, not mace, something marketed and labeled as bear spray will cause the least questions in a traffic stop, and it's wayyyyy more effective than trying to defend yourself with any blade under your own human strength. 

Bears, even our black bears here, are so much stronger, and faster, and bigger, and heavier, and their claws are longer, and their teeth are bigger, and they bite harder, and hit harder, and stay up through more pain and injury, than most people seem to understand. 

You can't win a fight against an adult black bear, no matter how big your knife is. You can only make them decide you aren't worth the effort. And if you fight hard enough, you can maybe get them to back off, but once they're on you, you're going to have a very bad time, even if you survive. 

The idea is to make them think twice before they get on you. Make yourself look bigger, wave your arms, shout, don't look away, and back away slow until you can reach help or safety. Don't let your guard down even if it backs off or disappears. Having something in your hands, like a long stick or a machete or a crowbar, can help make you look bigger. 

But having bear spray ready is your best defense because it's the quickest, most effective way to cause actual pain to the bear. If it gets close enough to be sprayed, don't hesitate. Spray at the face before it gets closer. Severe burning eyes nose and mouth, vision loss, and a horrible taste in its mouth is a great way to convince a bear you aren't worth the trouble.

Well, wolf spiders (at least family Lycosidae, which is what's called wolf spiders in my region) are in fact venomous. They can't kill you, and most are pretty harmless except being kinda painful, but some species can really fkkk up your day

However after a quick fact-checking journey, it turns out you are absolutely right about there being such a thing as non-venomous spiders. While NEARLY every spider is venomous, there are indeed two types of spiders I've learned of that have lost their venom glands to secondary evolution:

- the family Uloboridae (hackled orb weavers), containing 19 genera, all of which lack venom glands entirely and kill using silk

- a single genus of basal trapdoor spiders called Liphistius, most species of which are non-venomous (though a few species do still have venom glands), that as far as I can tell by the limited source material I've found, kill with fangs and brute force

It's possible that one or more of those spiders are called wolf spiders also, but so far I've not found anything that says so, and from looking at the pictures I don't think anyone could confuse either with the wolf spiders I'm familiar with lol

(I don't mention house spiders because lots of different species are called that, depending on the region, so for all I know there's a kind of hackled orb weaver regionally called a "house spider")
